title: What is HyperShift & Why It Exists
about: Imagine running hundreds of OpenShift clusters but instead of each needing its own set of master nodes, all control planes share one big cluster as pods. That is HyperShift — it decouples the control plane from workers, cutting provisioning from 30-45 min to ~10-15 min.
key_points: Standalone OCP: every cluster needs 3+ master nodes just for the control plane
HyperShift: control planes run as regular pods on a shared management cluster
Guest clusters have ZERO master nodes — only workers
This is the foundation behind ROSA HCP (AWS) and ARO HCP (Azure)
why_it_matters: This architecture is the core of everything our team builds. Every bug, feature, and design decision traces back to this decoupling. When a cluster has issues, the control plane pods live on the management cluster, not the guest.
explore_hint: Compare the 'Standalone OpenShift' vs 'HyperShift Model' table in Section 1 of the onboarding guide.

title: Core CRDs: HostedCluster, HostedControlPlane, NodePool
about: Three Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) define everything in HyperShift. Think of HostedCluster as the user saying 'I want a cluster', HostedControlPlane as the system's internal blueprint for building it, and NodePool as 'give me N worker nodes for that cluster'.
key_points: HostedCluster (HC): user-facing, lives in 'clusters' namespace, declares cluster intent
HostedControlPlane (HCP): internal, lives in CP namespace, CPO reads it to deploy components
NodePool (NP): user-facing, defines worker nodes, references an HC via spec.clusterName
HC -> HCP is 1:1, HC -> NP is 1:many
why_it_matters: These three CRDs are the API surface you will work with daily. Every controller, every status condition, every bug report maps back to one of these. Understanding which is user-facing vs internal prevents confusion when debugging.
explore_hint: Open each type file and compare their Spec structs. Notice how HCP spec mirrors HC spec.

title: Glossary: Management Cluster, Guest Cluster, CP Namespace
about: HyperShift splits responsibilities between two clusters: the management cluster runs all the operators and control plane pods, while the guest cluster is what end users consume and only has worker nodes. Each hosted cluster gets its own isolated namespace for its control plane components.
key_points: Management Cluster: runs HyperShift operators + all CP pods for every hosted cluster
Guest Cluster: the end-user cluster — only has worker nodes, no masters
CP Namespace: auto-created as '{hc-namespace}-{hc-name}' (e.g., clusters-my-cluster)
HyperShift Operator lives in 'hypershift' namespace, user CRs in 'clusters'
why_it_matters: When troubleshooting, knowing where to look is half the battle. CP pods are on the management cluster, and each cluster's components are in its own CP namespace. Run 'oc get pods -n clusters-<name>' to see everything.
explore_hint: Read the HostedControlPlaneNamespace() function in manifests.go — a simple but critical naming convention used everywhere.

title: Overall Architecture & Namespace Layout
about: The physical layout of HyperShift boils down to three namespaces on the management cluster. Understanding which namespace holds what is the fastest path to effective debugging — when something breaks, you need to know where to look.
key_points: 'hypershift' namespace: HyperShift Operator Deployment lives here
'clusters' namespace: user creates HostedCluster and NodePool CRs here
'clusters-<name>' namespace: auto-created, contains HCP + all CP components
Kubeconfig and kubeadmin-password Secrets are placed in the user namespace
why_it_matters: When a customer reports an issue, you will immediately go to 'clusters-<name>' to inspect CP pods. This namespace layout is the physical manifestation of the architecture.
explore_hint: On a running cluster, try: oc get ns | grep clusters and then oc get pods -n clusters-<name>.

title: The Operator Hierarchy: HO -> CPO -> 40+ Components
about: HyperShift uses a two-layer operator model. The HyperShift Operator (HO) is the top-level manager that watches user CRs and sets up each cluster's namespace. Inside each namespace, the Control Plane Operator (CPO) takes over and manages ~40 individual control plane components.
key_points: HO runs once on the management cluster, manages ALL hosted clusters
CPO runs once per hosted cluster, inside each CP namespace
HO creates: CP namespace, HCP CR, CPO Deployment, CAPI manager + provider
CPO deploys: etcd, KAS, KCM, scheduler, oauth-server, CVO, +30 more
why_it_matters: When something breaks, you need to know which operator is responsible. HO problems affect cluster-level operations (creation, deletion). CPO problems affect individual components (KAS down, etcd issues). Different operators, different logs, different fixes.
explore_hint: Look at registerComponents() function (~line 236 in hostedcontrolplane_controller.go) to see the full list of ~40 components.

title: HyperShift Operator (HO) — The 5 Controllers
about: The HyperShift Operator is not a single controller — it bundles 5 controllers, each responsible for a different aspect of cluster management. The HostedCluster and NodePool controllers are the two you will interact with most, handling cluster lifecycle and worker node management respectively.
key_points: HostedCluster controller: the big one (~5200 lines), manages full lifecycle
NodePool controller: manages CAPI machines, ignition tokens, rolling upgrades
HostedClusterSizing: decides resource allocations based on cluster size
Scheduler: places hosted clusters on management cluster nodes
SharedIngress: manages shared ingress routes across multiple hosted clusters
why_it_matters: Most of your code changes will touch one of these 5 controllers. The HC and NP controllers are where you will spend 80% of your time. Understanding which controller owns what prevents you from looking in the wrong place.
explore_hint: Start with the Reconcile() method (~line 337) in the HC controller. Follow the key sub-functions: reconcileHostedControlPlane(), reconcileControlPlaneOperator().

title: Control Plane Operator (CPO) — Managing 40 Components
about: The CPO is the workhorse that runs inside each cluster's CP namespace. It reads the HostedControlPlane CR like a blueprint and deploys everything needed: etcd for storage, KAS for the API, scheduler, controllers, networking, and more. The dependency chain matters — components start in a specific order.
key_points: One CPO instance per hosted cluster — runs as a Deployment in the CP namespace
Reads the HostedControlPlane CR to know what to deploy and configure
4 components start without KAS: etcd, PKI, featuregate-generator, router
Everything else waits for KAS to be available before starting
Deploys ~40 control plane components with dependency ordering
why_it_matters: The CPO is where most control plane bugs surface. If KAS is down, nothing else can start. If etcd is unhealthy, KAS cannot start. Understanding the dependency chain is key to root-causing control plane failures.
explore_hint: Find registerComponents() to see the full component list. Then look at the dependency graph in Section 6.2 of the onboarding guide.

title: CPOv2 Framework — The Declarative Component Model
about: Instead of writing reconciliation logic from scratch for each of the 40 components, HyperShift uses a declarative framework called CPOv2. You describe what a component needs (dependencies, config, sidecars) using a builder pattern, and the framework handles the rest — reconciliation, status tracking, and ordering.
key_points: Builder pattern: NewDeploymentComponent(name).WithDependencies(...).Build()
Predicates: enable/disable components based on cluster config
Dependencies: block reconciliation until dependent components are ready
Auto-injections: token minter sidecar, konnectivity proxy
Each component gets a ControlPlaneComponent CR with Available/RolloutComplete conditions
why_it_matters: When adding or modifying a control plane component, you use this framework. Understanding the builder pattern lets you contribute new components quickly without reinventing reconciliation logic.
explore_hint: Compare a simple component (v2/kube_scheduler/) with a complex one (v2/kas/) to see how the framework scales.

title: PKI Operator — Certificate Management
about: Every secure connection in a hosted cluster relies on certificates — API server TLS, etcd peer communication, kubelet authentication. The PKI operator manages all of this automatically: rotating CAs, signing CSRs, and handling the break-glass access mechanism that lets SREs access clusters in emergencies.
key_points: CertRotation controller: auto-rotates CAs and leaf certs using library-go
CertificateSigning: signs CSRs for break-glass access (emergency cluster access)
Two break-glass signers: Customer (tenant admin) and SRE (Red Hat support)
CSR Approval: auto-approves CSRs matching known signer patterns
All PKI sub-controllers are wired together in operator.go
why_it_matters: Certificate issues cause some of the most confusing failures — components cannot communicate, API servers reject connections. Understanding the PKI operator helps you debug TLS errors and certificate rotation issues.
explore_hint: Start with operator.go to see how all sub-controllers are wired together. Then look at certificates/ for signer definitions.

title: Ignition Server — How Worker Nodes Bootstrap
about: When a new worker node boots, it is a blank machine that needs to know how to configure itself. The Ignition Server solves this — it is an HTTPS server that generates and serves ignition configs (JSON documents describing the node's desired state) to new machines during their first boot.
key_points: NodePool controller creates a token Secret with: UUID, release image, config
TokenSecretReconciler generates ignition payload via MCO binaries
Payloads are cached in-memory with TTL (ExpiringCache)
Worker boots, calls GET /ignition with the token UUID as authorization
Node applies ignition, starts kubelet, and joins the guest cluster
why_it_matters: When worker nodes fail to join the cluster, the ignition flow is the first place to investigate. Common issues: token expired, ignition server unreachable, payload generation failed.
explore_hint: Start with start.go to understand the HTTP handler, then follow the flow into tokensecret_controller.go.

title: HostedCluster Creation Flow
about: Creating a hosted cluster is a multi-step orchestration between the HO and CPO. The HO sets up the stage — namespace, secrets, networking — and then the CPO takes over to deploy all the control plane components. Think of it as the HO building the house, and the CPO furnishing every room.
key_points: HO validates the HC spec (release image, config)
Creates CP namespace and copies secrets (pull-secret, SSH key, encryption key)
Creates HostedControlPlane CR, deploys CPO, CAPI Manager, and Provider
CPO then deploys etcd -> KAS -> +30 components in dependency order
HO copies kubeconfig Secret back to user namespace when ready
why_it_matters: When a cluster gets stuck during creation, you need to know which step failed. Is the CP namespace missing? Are secrets not copied? Is CPO crashing? Is etcd not starting? This flow is your debugging checklist.
explore_hint: Follow the creation flow: Reconcile() (~line 337) -> reconcileHostedControlPlane() (~line 2404) -> reconcileControlPlaneOperator().

title: Steady State & Upgrade Model
about: Once a cluster is running, HyperShift continuously reconciles to keep things healthy. The real power shows during upgrades — you can upgrade the control plane and workers independently. Change HC.spec.release for the control plane, change NP.spec.release for workers. They do not have to happen at the same time.
key_points: Steady state: CPO reconciles continuously, PKI rotates certs, NP manages nodes
Control plane upgrade: change HC.spec.release -> CPO deploys new component versions
Data plane upgrade: change NP.spec.release -> CAPI rolling update of workers
CP and data plane upgrades are fully independent
controlPlaneRelease: patches mgmt-side components without touching the data plane
why_it_matters: Decoupled upgrades are a major selling point of HyperShift. Customers can upgrade the control plane without disrupting workers, and vice versa. Understanding this model is critical when handling upgrade-related tickets.
explore_hint: Look for the 'controlPlaneRelease' field and the +rollout tags on NodePool spec fields.

title: HostedCluster Deletion Flow
about: Deleting a hosted cluster is not a simple 'kubectl delete' — it is an ordered teardown to prevent orphaned cloud resources. The HO systematically removes machines, waits for cloud cleanup, removes the control plane, and finally removes the finalizer. Getting this wrong means leaked cloud resources.
key_points: First: CAPI machines deleted, cloud instances terminated
Then: HCP deleted, CPO performs its own cleanup
Then: cloud resources cleaned up (load balancers, DNS, security groups)
Finally: cluster-wide RBAC removed, finalizer removed
destroy-grace-period annotation controls wait time before force-deleting
why_it_matters: Stuck deletions are one of the most common escalations. Check CloudResourcesDestroyed and HostedClusterDestroyed conditions to pinpoint which step is blocking.
explore_hint: The deletion flow starts at r.delete() (~line 501). Notice the conditions that track deletion progress.

title: CPO Reconciliation Flow — The Component Loop
about: The CPO's reconciliation is a pipeline: it fetches the HCP, runs pre-checks (etcd health, KMS validation, KAS availability), builds a context object, and then iterates through every registered component. Each component decides if it should run (predicate), checks if its dependencies are ready, and then reconciles.
key_points: Pre-checks: validate config, check etcd, validate KMS, check KAS
Core loop (~line 1232): iterate r.components, call c.Reconcile(cpContext)
Predicate check: should this component run for this cluster config?
Dependency check: are dependent components ready?
If predicate fails: component resources are deleted (disabled component)
why_it_matters: This is the main reconciliation loop that keeps every hosted cluster running. When a component misbehaves, understanding this flow helps determine if it is a dependency issue, a predicate issue, or a reconciliation bug.
explore_hint: Find the component iteration loop at ~line 1232. What happens when a component's dependency is not ready?

title: Component Dependencies & Status Propagation
about: Status in HyperShift flows upward like a chain: individual components report their health, the CPO aggregates these into HCP conditions, and the HO copies them to the HC that users see. When a customer says 'my cluster is degraded', you trace this chain backward to find the root cause.
key_points: KAS is the critical dependency — most components wait for it
7 components can start without KAS: etcd, featuregate-gen, CPO, CAPI, karpenter, router
Status chain: ControlPlaneComponent -> HCP conditions -> HC conditions
HC conditions visible to users: Available, Progressing, Degraded
checkDependencies() in status.go (~line 50) implements the dependency logic
why_it_matters: When a customer reports 'my cluster is degraded', follow the status chain backward: HC conditions <- HCP conditions <- ControlPlaneComponent CRs. This is your primary debugging technique.
explore_hint: Read checkDependencies() in status.go (~line 50), then look at hostedcluster_conditions.go for all condition types.

title: NodePool — Key Fields That Drive Behavior
about: The NodePool spec is how users control their worker nodes. Some fields are simple (replicas = how many nodes), but others have powerful side effects — changing spec.release or spec.config triggers a rolling replacement of all nodes. Fields tagged with +rollout are the ones that cause node replacement when changed.
key_points: spec.clusterName: immutable — once set, cannot be changed
spec.release: changing this triggers a rolling update of all nodes (+rollout tag)
spec.platform: cloud-specific config (AMI, instance type, disk size)
spec.replicas vs spec.autoScaling: manual count or min/max auto-scaling
spec.management.upgradeType: Replace (new machines) or InPlace
spec.config: MachineConfig references — changing also triggers rollout
why_it_matters: Misunderstanding which fields trigger rollouts leads to unexpected node replacement or stuck upgrades. Fields with +rollout tag are the critical ones to watch.
explore_hint: Search for the +rollout tag in nodepool_types.go. Why is spec.clusterName immutable?

title: Node Lifecycle — From NodePool to Running Worker
about: Getting a worker node from 'I want one' to 'it is running my pods' involves a surprisingly long chain: compute a config hash, create token and userdata secrets, tell CAPI to provision a machine, wait for the cloud to boot it, serve it an ignition config, and watch it join the cluster. Each step can fail independently.
key_points: ConfigGenerator.Hash() computes hash from MCO config + version + platform
Token Secret: contains token UUID, release image ref, compressed config
Userdata Secret: ignition stub pointing to ignition server URL with token
CAPI chain: MachineDeployment -> MachineSet -> Machine -> cloud instance
Instance boots, fetches ignition, applies it, starts kubelet, joins cluster
why_it_matters: When nodes do not join or get stuck, this end-to-end flow is your debugging roadmap. Check each step: Is the hash correct? Is the token valid? Is CAPI creating machines? Is the cloud provider failing?
explore_hint: Read these 4 files in order: nodepool_controller.go -> config.go -> token.go -> capi.go.

title: ClusterAPI Integration — The Resource Hierarchy
about: HyperShift does not talk to AWS, Azure, or KubeVirt directly for node management — it uses Cluster API (CAPI) as an abstraction layer. NodePool creates CAPI resources, and CAPI talks to the cloud provider. This means you need to distinguish between HyperShift bugs and CAPI bugs when node provisioning fails.
key_points: Resource chain: NodePool -> MachineDeployment -> MachineSet -> Machine
Platform-specific templates: AWSMachineTemplate, AzureMachineTemplate, etc.
MachineHealthCheck monitors machine health for auto-repair
Rolling updates triggered by DataSecretName change on MachineDeployment
All CAPI resources live in the CP namespace
why_it_matters: CAPI is a third-party project with its own lifecycle. When node provisioning fails, check Machine.status for cloud provider errors — the issue might be in CAPI, not HyperShift.
explore_hint: Look at awsMachineTemplateSpec() in aws.go to see how AMI, instance type, and security groups are configured.

title: Auto-scaling & Auto-repair
about: HyperShift supports multiple ways to scale nodes and automatically recover from failures. Manual scaling is simple, but Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter add intelligence. Auto-repair uses MachineHealthCheck to detect unhealthy nodes and replace them, with a safety valve (MaxUnhealthy=2) to prevent cascading deletions.
key_points: Manual: set spec.replicas, propagated to MachineDeployment
Cluster Autoscaler: spec.autoScaling.min/max becomes CAPI annotations
Karpenter: alternative auto-scaler, provisions directly from pending pods
MachineHealthCheck: detects unhealthy nodes (8 min cloud / 16 min agent timeout)
MaxUnhealthy=2: safety valve to prevent mass node replacement
why_it_matters: When nodes are not scaling or unhealthy nodes are not being replaced, understanding these mechanisms helps you debug. MaxUnhealthy=2 is especially important — it prevents mass node replacement during transient issues.
explore_hint: Find reconcileMachineHealthCheck() in capi.go (~line 649). Note the different timeouts for cloud vs Agent platforms.

title: Platform Interface — How HyperShift Abstracts Cloud Providers
about: HyperShift supports 7 cloud platforms through a clean Go interface. Every platform implements the same 6 methods: creating CAPI infra resources, deploying the provider, copying credentials, setting up encryption, defining RBAC, and cleaning up. This is the extension point for adding new platforms.
key_points: Platform interface: 6 methods every cloud provider must implement
ReconcileCAPIInfraCR: creates the cloud-specific CAPI infrastructure CR
ReconcileCredentials: copies cloud creds from user namespace to CP namespace
GetPlatform() dispatches to the correct implementation based on HC.spec.platform.type
7 platforms: AWS, Azure, KubeVirt, Agent, GCP, OpenStack, IBM Cloud/PowerVS
why_it_matters: This interface is how HyperShift stays cloud-agnostic. When working on platform-specific features, you implement or modify these methods. Understanding the interface makes cross-platform work predictable.
explore_hint: Read the Platform interface definition and GetPlatform() (~line 91) to see platform dispatch.

title: AWS Platform Deep Dive — Infrastructure & IAM
about: AWS is the primary platform powering ROSA HCP. Setting up a hosted cluster on AWS requires VPC networking, Route53 DNS zones, an S3 bucket for OIDC, and 6+ IAM roles using STS. Private clusters add VPC PrivateLink into the mix. Understanding this infrastructure is essential for debugging AWS-specific issues.
key_points: VPC with public/private subnets per availability zone
Route53: public zone (external DNS) + private zone (internal DNS)
S3 bucket hosts OIDC discovery documents for STS
6+ IAM roles: CCM, CAPA, CPO, EBS CSI, cloud-network-config, image-registry
PrivateLink: VPC endpoint services for private cluster connectivity
why_it_matters: AWS is the primary platform. IAM/OIDC issues are among the most common cloud-specific failures. Understanding the infra topology helps debug networking, DNS, and credential issues.
explore_hint: Look at AWSRolesRef (line 512 in aws.go) to see all IAM role ARNs that must be provided.

title: KubeVirt Platform — Nested Virtualization
about: KubeVirt lets you run hosted cluster workers as virtual machines on a Kubernetes cluster instead of cloud instances. This is useful for on-prem environments, development, and testing. The management cluster hosts CP pods while an infra cluster (can be the same) hosts the VMs as worker nodes.
key_points: Workers are KubeVirt VMs instead of cloud instances (EC2, Azure VMs, etc.)
Management cluster hosts CP pods; infra cluster hosts VMs (can be same cluster)
CDI DataVolumes provide root disks for VMs
KubevirtPlatformCredentials enables external infra cluster mode
No cloud IAM needed — uses in-cluster authentication
why_it_matters: KubeVirt is the go-to platform for on-prem and dev/test environments. It is also common in CI/CD. Understanding the dual-cluster mode (management vs infra) is essential for debugging VM provisioning issues.
explore_hint: Compare the KubeVirt platform implementation with the AWS one — notice how the Platform interface lets both share the same flow.

title: Cloud Controller Managers & Credential Management
about: Each cloud platform has its own Cloud Controller Manager (CCM) that runs as a CPOv2 component. Credentials follow a strict flow: users provide them in their namespace, the HO copies them to the CP namespace, and CPO components mount them. HyperShift never owns credentials — it only copies and uses them.
key_points: CCMs are CPOv2 components — one per platform, using the standard builder pattern
User provides credentials in the user namespace (alongside HC/NP CRs)
HO copies credentials to the CP namespace during reconciliation
CPO components mount credentials from the CP namespace
HyperShift NEVER manages/owns credentials — it copies and uses them
why_it_matters: Credential issues are a common source of problems, especially during rotation. The key insight: HyperShift does not manage credentials. If a credential is wrong, fix it in the user namespace and the HO will copy the update.
explore_hint: Compare the AWS CCM component with the KubeVirt CCM to see how the CPOv2 framework handles different platforms.

title: Multi-Module Structure — api/ Is a Separate Go Module
about: This catches almost every new contributor: the api/ directory is a separate Go module with its own go.mod. If you edit a type in api/ and try to build the main module, you will get 'undefined' errors because the vendored copy is stale. The fix is always 'make update'.
key_points: Root module: all operators, controllers, CLI, support packages
api/ module: separate go.mod, contains all CRD types and API definitions
Root consumes api/ via vendoring — changes in api/ need 'make update'
DO NOT modify vendor/ directories directly
GOLDEN RULE: always run 'make update' after editing anything in api/
why_it_matters: Forgetting 'make update' after api/ changes is the #1 time-waster for new contributors. You get confusing build errors that look like the code is wrong, but it is just the vendor copy being stale.
explore_hint: Read api/CLAUDE.md for critical API backward compatibility rules.

title: Main API Types — HostedCluster, HCP, NodePool, ControlPlaneComponent
about: The API types define the contract between users and the system. HostedClusterSpec (~line 529) is the single most important struct — it contains everything a user can configure. Understanding the relationship between these types (HC creates HCP, NP creates CAPI resources) is fundamental to all work.
key_points: HostedClusterSpec (~line 529): everything a user configures for their cluster
HostedClusterStatus (~line 2105): conditions, version info, kubeconfig ref
HCP spec mirrors HC spec — CPO reads HCP, not HC
ControlPlaneComponent: per-component status with Available/RolloutComplete
NodePoolSpec: release, platform, replicas, config — drives node behavior
why_it_matters: Every feature request, bug report, and API review requires understanding these types. The HostedClusterSpec is the single most important struct in the codebase.
explore_hint: Skim HostedClusterSpec starting at ~line 529 to understand what users can configure.

title: Feature Gates & Key Annotations
about: Feature gates control which API fields are available to users (e.g., Karpenter auto-scaling is behind a gate). Annotations are powerful operational levers that SREs use daily — override CPO images, force upgrades, trigger rolling restarts, adjust resource requests. These are defined at the top of hostedcluster_types.go.
key_points: Feature gates: +openshift:enable:FeatureGate=<Name> on API fields
Default vs TechPreviewNoUpgrade feature sets
Key annotations: control-plane-operator-image, restart-date, force-upgrade-to
resource-request-override: per-container resource overrides for CP components
All annotations defined in hostedcluster_types.go (lines 29-449)
why_it_matters: Feature gates determine what users can configure. Annotations are used daily by SREs during incidents — knowing these saves time. The resource-request-override annotation alone has saved many clusters from OOM issues.
explore_hint: Read the annotation constants block at the top of hostedcluster_types.go (lines 29-449).

title: Essential Development Commands
about: HyperShift has a rich Makefile with targets for building, testing, and verifying code. The most important command is 'make verify' — it runs the same checks CI does, so running it locally before pushing saves you from failed PR checks. The second most important is 'make update' after api/ changes.
key_points: make build: builds all binaries
make test: runs unit tests with race detection
make verify: MUST run before every PR (generate + fmt + vet + lint + codespell + gitlint)
make lint-fix: auto-fixes most linting issues
make update: regenerates everything after api/ changes
why_it_matters: CI will reject your PR if 'make verify' does not pass. Running it locally before pushing saves time and review cycles. These commands are your daily workflow.
explore_hint: Run 'make verify' on a clean checkout to see what it checks.

title: Workflow for API Changes
about: Changing an API type is the most impactful change you can make — it affects every consumer of the HyperShift API. The workflow is strict: edit types, regenerate everything, verify consistency, and add serialization tests if you changed a field type. Every API change must be safe for both upgrades (N+1) and rollbacks (N-1).
key_points: Step 1: Edit types in api/hypershift/v1beta1/
Step 2: make update (regenerate CRDs, vendor, clients, docs)
Step 3: make verify (check consistency)
Step 4: Add serialization compatibility test if field type changed
Rule: every API change must be safe for N+1 and N-1 compatibility
why_it_matters: Getting API compatibility wrong can break upgrades for thousands of clusters. The serialization test pattern catches these issues early. Never remove or rename fields.
explore_hint: Look at nodepool_types_test.go for the serialization compatibility test pattern.

title: Running Locally & CLI Structure
about: You can run the HyperShift operator locally against a real cluster for development. The CLI (built from main.go) provides subcommands for creating clusters, nodepools, and infrastructure. Understanding the CLI structure helps you test changes and set up development environments.
key_points: make hypershift-install-aws-dev: installs HyperShift in dev mode
make run-operator-locally-aws-dev: runs operator locally against a cluster
CLI entry point: main.go at repo root
cmd/cluster/: create/destroy cluster subcommands
cmd/install/assets/hypershift-operator/: final CRD YAML files
why_it_matters: Running locally is how you develop and test changes. The CLI is also how you set up test environments. Understanding the structure helps you add new subcommands or modify existing flows.
explore_hint: Try: bin/hypershift --help to see all available subcommands.

title: Upsert Pattern & Controller Structure
about: All HyperShift controllers follow the same structure: fetch resource, handle deletion, add finalizer, reconcile sub-resources, update status. The Upsert pattern wraps Kubernetes CreateOrUpdate to prevent reconciliation loops caused by server-defaulted fields. Learn one controller, and you can navigate all of them.
key_points: Upsert wraps CreateOrUpdate with loop detection to prevent infinite reconciliation
Standard pattern: fetch -> deletion check -> finalizer -> reconcile -> status update
CreateOrUpdateProvider interface injected into all controllers
All controllers follow the same structure — large or small
Compare HC controller (~5200 lines) vs HostedClusterSizing (much smaller)
why_it_matters: Reconciliation loops are a common bug in controller development. The upsert pattern prevents them. The standard structure means you can navigate any controller once you learn the pattern.
explore_hint: Read upsert.go, then compare the HC controller with the smaller HostedClusterSizing controller.

title: Test Conventions & API Backward Compatibility
about: HyperShift follows strict conventions for tests and API safety. Test names use Gherkin syntax ('When X it should Y'), assertions use gomega. API changes must never break existing clusters — every field change must be safe for upgrades and rollbacks. These conventions are enforced in PR reviews.
key_points: Test names: Gherkin syntax — 'When <condition> it should <expected behavior>'
Assertions: use gomega (Expect(x).To(Equal(y)))
Unit tests: *_test.go alongside source; E2E in test/e2e/
API: never remove/rename fields, always backward-safe
Changing value type to pointer requires omitempty tag
why_it_matters: PR reviews will flag incorrect test naming and missing compatibility tests. Following these conventions from day one means fewer review cycles.
explore_hint: Browse test/e2e/ for real E2E tests. Look at any *_test.go file for unit test examples.

title: Architectural Invariants — The 8 Design Rules
about: These 8 invariants are the 'constitution' of HyperShift — they are the rules that every design decision, PR review, and architecture choice is measured against. Violating them causes security issues, cascading failures, or upgrade breakage. Internalize them.
key_points: 1. Communication only flows management -> hosted, NEVER reverse
2. Workers only run user workloads + kubelet, konnectivity-agent, CNI
3. Guest cluster cannot modify HyperShift-managed features
4. Worker issues do not cascade to control plane lifecycle
5. HyperShift copies credentials, never manages/owns them
6. Each CP namespace is isolated via NetworkPolicies
7. CP and data plane upgrade independently
8. HO checks CPO image labels before enabling features (version compat)
why_it_matters: Every design review and PR review checks against these rules. Violating rule #1 (unidirectional communication) is a security risk. Violating rule #8 (CPO backward compat) breaks upgrades. These are non-negotiable.
explore_hint: Think about rule #8: why does the HO need to check CPO image labels before enabling features?

title: Key File Reference — Your Navigation Map
about: The HyperShift codebase has ~65 key files organized into 8 categories: APIs, HO Controllers, CPO Controllers, Framework, Platforms, PKI/Ignition, CLI, and Tests. This is your codebase GPS — when you get a bug report or review a PR, this map tells you which files are relevant.
key_points: APIs: 12 key files — types, conditions, platform specs, feature gates
HO Controllers: 15 files — HC controller, NP controller + config/token/capi
CPO Controllers: 8 files — HCP controller, v2 components
Framework: 5 files — controlplane-component core, builder, status, upsert
Priority system: Must read (week 1-4), Good to know (week 5-6), Reference (as needed)
why_it_matters: This is your codebase GPS. When you get a bug report, this map tells you which file to open. Bookmark Section 13 in the onboarding guide for quick reference.
explore_hint: Use the priority levels from Section 13: 'Must read' for month 1, 'Good to know' for month 2.

title: Learning Paths — Control Plane, Data Plane, Platform
about: After 7 weeks of daily topics, use these structured reading paths for deeper code-level understanding. Three paths: Control Plane (follow HC -> HCP -> CPO -> component), Data Plane (follow NP -> config -> token -> CAPI -> ignition), Platform (follow interface -> implementation -> CCM -> API types). Pick the one matching your work area.
key_points: Control Plane path: 6 files, follow HC -> HCP -> CPO -> component
Data Plane path: 6 files, follow NP -> config -> token -> CAPI -> ignition
Platform path: 5 files, follow interface -> impl -> CCM -> API types
Each path builds understanding incrementally — read in order
Control plane path recommended first — HC -> HCP is 80% of the work
why_it_matters: Structured learning beats random exploration. After these daily topics, these paths give you a clear sequence for going deeper in your area of focus.
explore_hint: Pick the path matching your current work. The control plane path is recommended first.

title: Tips for New Team Members — Putting It All Together
about: Congratulations — you have completed the 7-week HyperShift onboarding journey! These 7 tips distill everything into actionable habits. The best way to solidify this knowledge now is to start contributing: pick a bug, write a fix, run make verify, and open your first PR.
key_points: Tip 1: HC, HCP, NP — learn these CRDs deeply, they are 80% of the work
Tip 2: Data flows HC->HCP->Components and NP->CAPI->Cloud->Node
Tip 3: .status.conditions tells you what is happening — always check them
Tip 4: make verify before every push
Tip 5: oc get pods -n clusters-<name> shows all CP components at a glance
Tip 6: Tests are the best docs — read *_test.go and test/e2e/
Tip 7: hypershift dump (cmd/dump/) captures full cluster state for debugging
why_it_matters: You now have a mental map of the entire HyperShift codebase. Go build something! Start with a bug fix or small feature — the best way to learn is by doing.
explore_hint: This is the last daily topic! Pick a Jira bug and start contributing.
